newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten swansong defends HK democracy, rights.
newsitem.headline: Patten swansong defends HK democracy, rights.

text.p: British Governor Chris Patten, in a swansong annual policy speech on Wednesday, firmly defended Hong Kong's fledgling democracy and human rights, and warned that if China erased them it would destabilise the territory.

In a far-reaching 95-minute speech to the Legislative Council, Patten came closer than ever to accusing China of violating an international treaty through its plan to appoint a new "provisional legislature" and scrap Legco.

At the same time the former British Conservative Party chairman served loud notice that he intended to be no lame duck in his final 272 days as governor, and that Britain would rule its last major colony "full steam ahead" to the last minute, until midnight next June 30.
"Britain has made clear repeatedly to Chinese leaders that it would be wrong and damaging to scrap this council and replace it with a non-elected body.

"That remains our unshakeable position," Patten said. "We believe that there is no reason why this Council should not be allowed to serve the full four-year term for which it was elected," he said. The council was elected a year ago.
Patten said a provisional legislature allowed to operate before next July 1 would be unnecessarily provocative and destabilising, and could lead to legal challenges in court.
"We will have nothing to do with it. We will not assist a provisional legislature's establishment, operation or its ability to withstand legal challenge," the governor said.
The issue has been at the heart of bitter quarrels between Britain and China in recent years in the course of negotiations on handover details, although relations have thawed lately.

China accuses Britain of overstepping a 1984 handover deal through electoral reforms introduced by Patten after he arrived in 1992. Britain views China's plan to dismantle Legco and to install an appointed legislature in a similar vein but has avoided saying explicitly that it would be "illegal".
Patten, however, came very close to doing so on Wednesday.

"He was very adamant about having nothing to do with a provisional legislature. The explanation was very strong that a provisional Legco would be a breach of the Joint Declaration," said political analyst Michael DeGolyer.
But Patten upset the territory's pro-democracy camp for not going far enough. They wanted real action against China.

"Mr Patten dislikes being called a lame duck but he has ducked the issues of greatest concern to Hong Kong people -- the continuation of our elected legislature and rule of law," said Martin Lee, leader of Hong Kong's biggest party, the Democrats.
"It is not sufficient to defend democracy and the rule of law through words alone. It must be by deeds as well," Lee said.
"Hong Kong's most pressing legal and constitutional problems are being swept under the carpet."

Patten, Britain's 28th governor of Hong Kong, took on the job of steering the capitalist outpost of 6.3 million people towards Chinese rule in mid-1997 after losing his parliamentary seat in Britain's last general election.
In his speech he also assailed China's criticisms of a Bill of Rights he introduced in Hong Kong, and he challenged the idea Hong Kong people do not care about human rights and politics.

He noted that over the decades of communist rule in China, "wave after wave of refugees swam, walked, ran and climbed over barbed wire to find a new life" in Hong Kong and "the peace and safety guaranteed by the rule of law".

Although he has less than nine months left in charge, he made clear he intends to keep his hand on the helm by defiantly brandishing a raft of new policy measures to improve the quality of life, and was confident Hong Kong would continue to thrive.
"I hope that Hong Kong will take tomorrow by storm. And when it does, History will stand and cheer," he said.
